extraction_notes.note: Wrong \refs: the proof of Theorem 19 says 'under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{suprt}' (Theorem 21), the proof of Proposition 22 cites 'Lemma~\ref{suprtrdpf}' meaning Lemma 16, and the proof of Theorem 7 calls itself 'Proposition~\ref{openlrdp}'. These ref edges are marked mention; the intended Lemma 16 edge was added as inferred.

Hahn-Banach Theorem (superlinear-minorant version) kept origin paper: the paper calls it a 'natural extension of a well-known result' without attribution and gives only a proof sketch (rigor semi_formal); it may well be classical (Hahn-Banach-Kantorovich).

Section 3 says its arguments are 'mostly based on' Aliprantis-Tourky's Cones and Duality, so the RK transform definition and its basic properties are marked external although the paper proves them; the L-RDP results there are kept paper.
Proposition 12 has no proof environment; the two sentences before it ('Observe that ... leads to the following useful observation.') are its argument and were made a prose proof node.
The R^3 example spans the figure float and its caption between its announcement and its description; kept as one example node.

nodes.statement: Let us give a sketch of the proof. By the standard inductive reasoning it is sufficient to consider the case dim X slash L = 1. We fix some x_0 in X setminus L; then X = \x + s x_0 mid x in L, s in mathbb R\ and we need to define a value y_0 in Y in such a way that an extension T (x + s x_0) = T_0 x + s y_0 would satisfy the necessary estimate T (x + s x_0) geqslant p (x + s x_0) whenever x + s x_0 in X_+. Considering different signs of s we see that this is equivalent to T_0 u - p (u - x_0) geqslant y_0 geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v for all u, v in L satisfying u - x_0 in X_+ and v + x_0 in X_+. Observe that such u and v always exist since by the assumptions X_+ + L = X = -X = -(X_+ + L) = -X_+ - L = -X_+ + L, and for any such u and v we have u + v = (u - x_0) + (v + x_0) in X_+ cap L, so T_0 u + T_0 v = T_0 (u + v) geqslant p (u + v) = p ([u - x_0] + [v + x_0]) geqslant p (u - x_0) + p (v + x_0) by superlinearity of p, which implies that T_0 u - p (u - x_0) geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v for any u, v in L satisfying u - x_0 in X_+ and v + x_0 in X_+. From it is clear that the set of values of the right-hand part of~ has an upper bound, and the least upper bound of the right-hand part is also a lower bound for the left-hand part. Thus we may set y_0 = sup \p (v + x_0) - T_0 v mid v + x_0 in X_+\ and conclude that y_0 satisfies the required estimates~.

Let us give a sketch of the proof. 
By the standard inductive reasoning it is sufficient to consider the case
$\dim X \slash L = 1$.  We fix some $x_0 \in X \setminus L$;
then $X = \{x + s x_0 \mid x \in L, s \in \mathbb R\}$ and
we need to define a value $y_0 \in Y$ in such a way that an extension
$T (x + s x_0) = T_0 x + s y_0$ would satisfy the necessary estimate
$T (x + s x_0) \geqslant p (x + s x_0)$ whenever $x + s x_0 \in X_+$.
Considering different signs of $s$ we see that this is equivalent to
\begin{equation}
\label {hbk}
T_0 u - p (u - x_0) \geqslant y_0 \geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v
\end{equation}
for all $u, v \in L$ satisfying $u - x_0 \in X_+$ and $v + x_0 \in X_+$.
Observe that such $u$ and $v$ always exist since
by the assumptions
$$
X_+ + L = X = -X = -(X_+ + L) = -X_+ - L = -X_+ + L,
$$
and for any such $u$ and $v$ we have $u + v = (u - x_0) + (v + x_0) \in X_+ \cap L$, so
$$
T_0 u + T_0 v = T_0 (u + v) \geqslant p (u + v) = p ([u - x_0] + [v + x_0]) \geqslant p (u - x_0) + p (v + x_0)
$$
by superlinearity of $p$, which implies that
\begin{equation}
\label {hbk1}
T_0 u - p (u - x_0) \geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v
\end{equation}
for any $u, v \in L$ satisfying $u - x_0 \in X_+$ and $v + x_0 \in X_+$.
From \eqref {hbk1} it is clear that the set of values of the right-hand part of~\eqref {hbk}
has an upper bound, and the least upper bound of the right-hand part is also a lower bound for the left-hand part.
Thus we may set
$$
y_0 = \sup \{p (v + x_0) - T_0 v \mid v + x_0 \in X_+\}
$$
and conclude that $y_0$ satisfies the required estimates~\eqref {hbk}.

Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, $X_+$ is a generating cone in $X$,
$Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice and $\mathcal L$ is a linear space of operators from $X$ to $Y$
satisfying $\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {Y}$.
Suppose also that either the following assumptions is satisfied.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$Y = \mathbb R$; we set $X_r = X_+$ in this case.
\item
$\mathrm{int} X_+ \neq \emptyset$ and $Y$ is Archimedean; we set $X_r = \{0\} \cup \mathrm{int} X_+$ in this case.
\end{enumerate}
Then the following conditions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\mathcal L$ is a lattice.
\item
$\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property.
\item
The Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$ of any finite collection~$T$ of operators from $\mathcal L$ is linear on $X_r$.
\item
For any operator $T \in \mathcal L$ the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rktps {T}$ is linear on $X_r$.
\item
$X$ ordered by the cone $X_r$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, if any (and therefore all) of these conditions are satisfied then $\mathcal L = \rlinop {X} {Y}$
and $\sup T = \rkts {T}$ in $\mathcal L$ on $X_r$ for any finite collection of operators $T \subset \mathcal L$.
